problem: Existing synthetic data pipelines for embodied AI are fragmented and task-specific (navigation or manipulation only), causing duplicated engineering, non-transferable optimizations, and instability (hangs, no cluster scheduling or fault tolerance) in long-running large-scale generation.
motivation: Scaling data volume and diversity is key for foundation models, and real-world collection is too costly. Synthetic generation is a scalable alternative, but monolithic pipelines couple CPU-bound planning, GPU-bound rendering and I/O-bound storage serially, wasting hardware. Silent simulator hangs also break sustained cluster runs.
key_idea: Nimbus is a unified four-layer framework (Components, Stage Runner, Schedule Opt, Backend Opt) that expresses navigation and manipulation pipelines in a common Load-Plan-Render-Store lifecycle. It decouples the stages asynchronously and adds dynamic scheduling, global load balancing, a supervisor for fault tolerance, and renderer-specific optimizations.
insight: Speedups come from architectural efficiency (overlapping CPU/GPU/I-O and faster renderers), not from reducing per-frame computation. Per-stage latencies stay comparable to the baseline, but end-to-end latency becomes bounded by the bottleneck stage. The paper reports a 2.1-3.2x speedup, and Nav-Mesh render latency drops from 446.29 to 159.46 ms. For navigation, where planning is light, full decoupling is not worthwhile because of serialization/IPC overhead, so only I/O masking and renderer optimization are applied. Scaling from 8 to 128 GPUs reaches about 86% linear efficiency, limited by tail effects and by too few tasks per GPU for the load balancer.
method: Stage Runner Layer: standard Load-Plan-Render-Store lifecycle with abstract iterators BaseLoader, BaseRandomizer, BasePlanner, BaseRenderer and BaseWriter (Parquet output).

Components Layer: navigation components (GSMeshLoader, NavPlanner with A*, SCGSRenderer, BlenderProcRenderer, NavWriter) with a proxy-mesh pipeline for Gaussian Splatting assets. Manipulation uses Env adapter components plus a Workflow API (GenManipWorkflow, SimBoxWorkflow).
Pipeline parallelism: planner (CPU) and renderer (GPU) processes are decoupled via message queues, and an async I/O thread pool batches writes to hide storage latency.
Dynamic pipeline scheduling: when a planner exhausts its tasks, the scheduler reclaims its resources and spawns extra renderers that join the existing queue, reducing tail latency.

Global load balancer and Supervisor: a Master-Worker design (WorkerManager, TaskManager, heartbeats, lazy context loading), plus an out-of-band Ray-managed Supervisor that SIGKILLs hung workers so Ray respawns them, turning silent hangs into fail-stop errors.

Backend optimizations: Blender runs a GPU-resident OptiX pipeline (RT cores for ray tracing, Tensor cores for denoising) with multi-process rendering to bypass the GIL. Isaac Sim uses stacked rendering, mapping temporal states to spatial sub-regions in a single pass. Gaussian Splatting integrates FlashGS and TC-GS kernels.

setting.backbone: none (systems framework built on Ray with Blender/BlenderProc, Isaac Sim, Sapien and Gaussian Splatting renderers)
setting.observation: synthetic multi-view RGB, depth and segmentation rendered from simulators
setting.action_space: not applicable (data generation; A* trajectories for navigation, end-effector waypoints with CuRobo for manipulation)
setting.simulator: Blender/BlenderProc, Isaac Sim, Sapien, 3D Gaussian Splatting renderers
setting.privileged: uses privileged scene meshes and asset annotations for planning (as data generation), no test-time policy

numbers_note: No navigation benchmark metrics; the evaluation reports systems throughput (speedups of 2.1x-3.2x, Nav-Mesh render latency 446.29 ms to 159.46 ms, ~86% scaling efficiency from 8 to 128 GPUs), mostly given in figures.
results: Nimbus achieves 2.1x-3.2x end-to-end speedup over unoptimized baselines on four pipelines (Nav-GS, Nav-Mesh, GenManip, SimBox). Nav-Mesh render latency falls 64% (446.29 to 159.46 ms), and the ~56 ms/frame I/O latency is fully masked. In 24-hour runs on 8-128 RTX 4090 GPUs it reaches ~86% linear scaling efficiency with no node or task failures.
limitations: Evaluation compares only against its own unoptimized baseline, with no comparison to other frameworks, and results are mostly in figures. It does not evaluate downstream policy quality.
Scaling efficiency drops (~86% at 128 GPUs) due to tail effects and small per-GPU task pools, and for navigation the plan stage is not decoupled because IPC overhead outweighs the benefit.
Planners, automated scene generation and task configuration are left as future work.
compares_to: Unoptimized baseline pipelines (InternData-N1 GS/Blender, InternData-A1, InternData-M1)
